lesson.menu_desc: Dialogue: the post-mortem call after a deal falls through, from regret to a plan -- 33 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 23 -- The Deal That Fell Through
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Pedro Monaco | Lesson 23 -- The Deal That Fell Through
lesson.grammar_point: wish, if only and would rather

listenings.text: A good post-mortem is not a trial. The goal is not to find out who dropped the ball. It is to find out where the process let the team down. So I ask every team to use three sentences, in this order. First, a regret: I wish we had done something differently. Keep it about the team, not about one person. Second, a lesson: what do we know now that we didn't know then? Third, a change: it's time we did something new. And the change has to be specific. It's time we communicated better means nothing. It's time we sent the client an update every Monday means something. One more rule. If somebody starts to dwell on the past, I stop the meeting for a minute and ask them to finish the sentence: so next time, we will... A post-mortem that ends without a change is just a complaint with a calendar invitation.

The biggest deal of my career fell through at the eleventh hour, and for a long time I blamed the other side. We had spent eight months negotiating the acquisition of a logistics company in Florida. Two days before closing, their lawyers disclosed a pending lawsuit from a former employee. It wasn't a huge claim, but our board lost confidence, and the deal was over. For weeks I kept thinking: if only they had told us earlier. Then my mentor asked me a question I didn't enjoy: did you ask them? The honest answer was no. Our checklist asked about litigation in general, but nobody had asked about employment claims. I wish I could say I fixed it the next day. I didn't. It took another near miss before I rewrote the checklist. Today, every new deal starts with forty questions, and the employment section comes first.

extra_audio.text: First, Laura tells Pedro that the Houston deal fell through on Friday. Then Pedro says he wishes they had started due diligence earlier. Next, Laura admits she regrets promising the board a closing date in June. After that, Pedro suggests checking every intermediary before the term sheet. Finally, Laura promises to call the sales team herself.
